Rugby Refereeing

By: Julian Sun | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
With so many controversial rugby referee decisions, we ask if the game we love so much has become too complicated.

Unique Selling Point:
Why are the laws of Rugby Union so open to interpretation? Are the laws too complicated? Is it asking too much of a single ref (and his assistants) to take charge in a game in which he needs to make hundreds of decisions over the course of 80 minutes?

Summary:
Rugby is one of the most supported sports in the world and continues to grow in popularity. A staggering 857 million people watched the 2019 Rugby World Cup in Japan.

It’s also become highly competitive with the Northern Hemisphere more than a match for the traditional powerhouses of world rugby, South Africa, Australia and New Zealand. So much so that games are now often decided by a single score.

With such fine margins, the influence of the referee is becoming more crucial as a single call can decide the outcome of a match.

But why is there such inconsistency in the way a game of rugby can be refereed?
Why are the laws of Rugby Union so open to interpretation? Are the laws too complicated? Is it asking too much of a single ref (and his assistants) to take charge in a game in which he needs to make hundreds of decisions over the course of 80 minutes?

Players come under intense pressure in the glare of the media spotlight, yet no scrutiny is allowed of the ref - according to World Rugby

But the advent of social media is throwing a microscope on the performance of referees. We saw it last year with the infamous Rassiegate video during last year’s British and Irish Lions tour of SA

Now Rassie is once again in trouble for pointing out referee inconsistencies and mistakes on twitter - and again he’s been banned for his troubles

Ahead of next year’s 2023 Rugby World Cup, what can be done to remedy the situation?

Expert:
Swys De Bruin
Victor Matfield
Freek Burger

Press Release:


Intense and filled of drama, rugby union is one of the biggest sports on the planet.

Currently, World Rugby has never been more competitive with traditional rivalries like the Springboks and the All Blacks often decided by a single score.

With such fine margins, referees hold the key to ensuring “fair play”.

With the rush of adrenaline in a physical contact sport, the performance of match officials is increasingly in the spotlight, with every controversial decision dissected and scrutinised.
With so much at stake and innovative technology advancements at their fingertips, why are some referees, still getting it wrong?


Script:


Rugby Referees - Script

INTRO
Xola V/O: As a broadcaster, I’ve had the privilege of covering the wonderful game of rugby union for almost 2 decades. I count myself as one of over half a billion fans that have made it one of the most popular sports in the world.

It’s easy to see why… At its best, it is a spectacle, filled with spectacular tries and nail-biting drama and while it continues to grow in popularity, it is also one of the hardest to referee.

LINK: The most important person on the rugby field is without a doubt the referee. Required to make hundreds of decisions in every game. If he’s had a good game, he’s rarely mentioned but should he get something wrong…

Xola V/O: The problem is that those mistakes are being pointed out more than ever in an age of social media and high-definition cameras.


EXAMPLES OF REFEREE INCONSISTENCIES
Victor Matfield: [00:02:52] Rugby's laws are probably the most complicated in any sport. I mean, there's so many laws at each breakdown. I can actually give a penalty every time, each way. And that's what makes it difficult. And that's what that's what make the good referees good. [00:03:09

V/O: Former Springbok Captain Victor Matfield knows the pressure modern referees face

Victor Matfield: [00:02:01] I think you can't get away with anything these days. I think in the past there was a lot of things that were missed, but it was missed both ways. Now TMO's, they come in, they show things and everything is under the microscope. [00:02:18][16.3]

V/O: Former Bok Attack coach Swys De Bruin agrees

Swys: [00:03:49] I've got a big problem though where I feel it happens of the slow motion. As soon as you freeze frame a down, it's a total different picture, like on a late tackle if I see that happens like that one prop in the Australia,the Italy game. Yeah he was playing coming around and and it was in the wrong channel in the live it was just sort of okay but if you freeze frame it, it looked ten times worse [00:04:40][20.8]

Italy v Australia 67th minute

Xola: [00:08:18] Whilst we’re on the Wallabies, they had a great match against the Boks. The Korobete tackle on Mapimpi was one and this probably talks to what you say when you mention playing something in slow motion versus real time.

Swys: [00:08:41] Absolutely. If no one had the luxury of slow motion Korobete’s one, no problem. But as soon as I slowed it down, I'm almost going from penalty to yellow to, is this not a red?

V/O: Another example involved Bok Flanker Pieter-Steph Du Toit who was inadvertently pushed by his own players into the face of French centre Jonathan Danty.

Up-sound of Pieter Steph Red Card: France v SA (10 minutes in)

Victor Matfield: [00:04:32] When I saw it, I knew it was going to be a red card because with what the law says at the moment, face to face with impact, unfortunately it’s a red card. [00:05:15][43.4]

Swys: [00:04:42] You know Pieter-Steph when in great body position what from a coaching point of view nothing wrong and then the timing of Kwagga as he and Damian Allende as they he to me and he couldn't stop himself now I could see it on his face I coach that guy, I know his passion. I know everything about him. There was no way in the world he's not a foul or dirty player. It's not in him.

Victor Matfield: [00:06:29] I think the focus should be on the IRB and the laws and why they making the laws. Yes, they want to keep the game safe. But I mean, we as rugby players, we make the decision to play this game. We know there's a risk of getting injured, getting maybe concussion. Break a leg. That's part of the game.

Red Card: France v SA (47 minutes in)

Xola: [00:11:49] I wonder if referees feel pressure to even the scale. So once they've given him penalty to one side almost wanting to even things out.

Swys: [00:12:25] For sure. The 50/50 calls and the pressure from the crowd and stuff will definitely lead him to that.

Victor Matfield: [00:05:36] I thought he looked at the ball, he was over the shoulder Can never be a red card because he was watching the ball he didn't even see. For me, the only time this should be a red card If there's intent and you want it to hit someone, you come from the side, you punch someone swinging arm straight to the neck or something like that. That should be a red card I think we have things is gone at this stage with red cards it's just absolutely crazy. [00:06:02][26.2]

V/O: And while Antoine Du Pont was given a red card for this incident, Bok star Cheslin Kolbe escaped with just a yellow card for a similar tackle against the British and Irish Lions.

Cutaway: Cheslin Kolbe takes out Connor Murray 27th minute SA v British Lions 2nd test

IS RUGBY TOO COMPLICATED?
V/O: So why are referees so inconsistent in the way they apply the laws? Freek Burger is a former international referee.

Freek Burger: [00:02:21] I think the main problem at this stage is too many laws. I'm going to take you back to the eighties when I refereed without a yellow card, without a red card, without without being being linked up to your touch judges. You were the sole judge of facts and law on the field, and you've got to produce. There's too many cooks spoiling the broth.

Swys: [00:07:02] You’ve got to simplify the game for starters, we have to have fewer laws, instead of eight things to focus at the line out, focus on two, three things because it's very very tough

Xola: [00:32:56] There seems to be so many things that referees could be picky about when it comes to scrums. [00:33:03][7.0]

Swys: [00:33:03] Oh yeah. I'll show you a little example. If I show you my hands like this and I ask you now I know which which side is going to collapse. Who's guilty? [00:33:29][25.4]

Xola: [00:33:30] Well, to me, it's a lottery. [00:33:30][0.9]

Swys: [00:33:31] I know it was my right end for obvious the ending from that side, and I pancaked, so I should be nailed. But it happened so quickly. It happens instantly. And he's got to make a decision.

Victor Matfield: [00:28:57] If you get someone in a box with a TMO that's a specialist in the front row, I think they will make much better decisions at Scrum-time. Once that scrum goes down, you can have two views before they get up and you can actually give a call through to the referee.

Freek Burger: [00:03:07] Remember it's 30 vs 1 and this poor guy in the middle, he's got to he's got to impress 30 players for 80 minutes and after the match, he goes into the field. He's got the 2 coaches to face.

RASSIE
V/O: Especially when a coach like Rassie Erasmus uses social media to spotlight referee mistakes.

Freek Burger: [00:12:14] I don't think Rassie’s the only coach in the world and it's got problems. I think all the coaches at the moment, if you take them and you asking the same question, they all they all have their problems about the rugby state of emergency.

Xola: [00:12:46] You've worked with him. You know very well. He's an incredibly passionate coach. Why do you think he's opted to use particularly social media, to get his message across?

Swys: [00:14:10] I truly believe that a lot of his stuff comes from his heart. everything for him is about the team and the hard stuff. And he really got involved so much with this fact that he wants to prove everyone wrong through social media. So if you ask me straight away, was Rassie, right? No, he was wrong. Use the protocol because you cannot, in my opinion, keep on going that route. And then he got warned and that and yet he carried on.

V/O: Even though Erasmus was banned for 2 games, relationships are seemingly on the mend. Last Thursday Rassie met with World Rugby for what has been described as “positive discussions around recent events and match official communications in general”

CLOSING
LINK: Ahead of next year’s World Cup, rugby has never been more competitive with games more often than not, being decided by a single score. This makes the decisions made by a referee more crucial than ever before.

Victor Matfield: [00:30:52], We've seen in the women's final World Cup, for the first time, women's rugby, 50,000 people in the stadium, millions of people watching it. again, 15 minutes into a game, a red card, 14 versus 15 and now you get 15 versus 14 for 60 minutes in a World Cup final. Don't want to see that.

Swys: [00:34:36] World rugby are making it much more technical and the answer is they should simply follow the old thing much more. Get few laws, fewer things and we might save our beautiful game.

PROMOS:

TEASER: In rugby the referee is the most important man on the pitch but with a recent spate of controversial decisions, their mistakes are being scrutinized like never before

PROMO 1: Tradition says that in the world of rugby union, the word of the referee is final.

PROMO 2: Rassie Erasmus has been banned again by world rugby for highlighting referee mistakes on twitter. But does he have a point?

PROMO 3: This is Ellis Park Stadium Springbok rugby’s fortress. When filled to capacity, it is one of the most imposing venues in world rugby. A partisan crowd can both inspire and intimidate players alike but what about a referee? After all they’re human too right?

metadata.Summary: Rugby is one of the most supported sports in the world and continues to grow in popularity. A staggering 857 million people watched the 2019 Rugby World Cup in Japan. It’s also become highly competitive with the Northern Hemisphere more than a match for the traditional powerhouses of world rugby, South Africa, Australia and New Zealand. So much so that games are now often decided by a single score. With such fine margins, the influence of the referee is becoming more crucial as a single call can decide the outcome of a match. But why is there such inconsistency in the way a game of rugby can be refereed? Why are the laws of Rugby Union so open to interpretation? Are the laws too complicated? Is it asking too much of a single ref (and his assistants) to take charge in a game in which he needs to make hundreds of decisions over the course of 80 minutes? Players come under intense pressure in the glare of the media spotlight, yet no scrutiny is allowed of the ref - according to World Rugby But the advent of social media is throwing a microscope on the performance of referees. We saw it last year with the infamous Rassiegate video during last year’s British and Irish Lions tour of SA Now Rassie is once again in trouble for pointing out referee inconsistencies and mistakes on twitter - and again he’s been banned for his troubles Ahead of next year’s 2023 Rugby World Cup, what can be done to remedy the situation?
